memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then he shall sacrifice the doves or the young pigeons, such as the person can afford, one as a sin offering and the other as a burnt offering, together with the grain offering. In this way the priest will make atonement before the LORD on behalf of the one to be cleansed. These are the regulations for anyone who has a defiling skin disease and who cannot afford the regular offerings for their cleansing." - Lev 14:30-32 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
There it is again — such as the person can afford. God says it twice in this chapter, as if He wants to be certain no one misses it.

And then look at the outcome in verse 31: in this way the priest will make atonement. Not a partial atonement. Not a provisional one. The same word, the same result.

Two birds accomplished what three lambs accomplished, because atonement never rested on the size of the gift. It rested on God's appointed way and God's willingness to accept.

That truth guards us from something dangerous. If atonement could be bought, the rich would be nearer to God than the poor, and the generous would be safer than the struggling. Religion often works that way. The gospel never does.

Jesus watched people putting large sums into the temple treasury, and then a widow dropped in two small coins. He said she had put in more than all the others (Mark 12:41-44). God does not weigh the amount. He sees the heart.

So bring what you have. A small faith, a tired prayer, a life that feels thin compared to others. Offered to God through Christ, it is received in full.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you secretly believe God values people by what they can give?
2. What "small offering" have you been ashamed to bring to God?
3. How does the widow's two coins encourage you today?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You measure the heart and not the amount. I bring You what I have, small as it seems, and trust that in Christ it is received. Amen.
